prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: B048 is the one candidate on the list where an original atomic-physics idea, a decisive experimental realisation and broad independent confirmation all line up. Katori's magic-wavelength insight removes the lattice light shift, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil broadening. Ye's group then took the strontium clock to the 10^-18 regime and showed that interactions in a many-body lattice are understood and controllable. Many laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others, with Sr, Yb and Hg) now run such clocks, and their comparisons agree, which is the robustness I look for. The results are fundamental and not merely technological: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter searches, with the redefinition of the second being prepared around these clocks. As with high-harmonic generation, a clean basic idea in atomic structure became a new way to see nature. The two-person credit is also the cleanest attribution of any entry on the list.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness. The frequency comb (2005) and the control of single trapped ions, including the Al+ ion clock (2012), are close neighbours, and a sceptical colleague can say this is the next step in a precision-time lineage that the Academy has already honoured twice. A second reservation is that it is an instrument and measurement advance, so a committee that wants a discovery of a new phenomenon may find it less striking than the quantum-classical boundary questions. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and credit for clocks outside the two names (Lemonde, Takamoto and the Yb and ion-clock groups) is not zero.

responses.point: Ranks B011 (KPZ universality with Takeuchi's experiment) first as a simple, universal mechanism with a bridge to random-matrix theory, and ranks B048 second while noting overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes.
responses.response: I agree that the overlap objection must be answered, not waved away. The 2005 prize was for the comb as a frequency ruler and the 2012 prize for single quantum systems and ion control. The lattice clock rests on a different idea, namely trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength where the light shift cancels, and it gives a different physical regime (many-body, 10^-18 stability). On KPZ I defer to you as a statistical physicist. The universality and Takeuchi's experiment are persuasive, but only one member ranked it, and three-name credit is awkward because Parisi, and the exact-solution authors, are outside the credit. I would like to hear how you would resolve that before it displaces a configuration with eight of eight members ranking B048.

responses.point: Ranks topological insulators (B019) first as a conceptually clean new class of matter, and B048 third, asking whether the lattice clock is a discovery or an instrumentation advance.
responses.response: I take the topological insulator case seriously, and it is the strongest candidate outside AMO physics. But three of its attribution questions are open: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe system, Fu, Kane and Mele plus Moore and Balents made the three-dimensional case, and the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases. As an atomic theorist I cannot adjudicate that priority; you can, and I would like you to say whether the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio is truly the clean decisive set. On your instrumentation point, the clock is an instrument, but its value is that it measures things nature does not otherwise show us (redshift over a millimetre, constancy of constants), which is how the 1989 and 2012 awards were framed too.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED (B001) first, flags the proximity to the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize, and puts B048 second with a concern about earlier clock-related prizes and about timing relative to the pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: Your own timing worry about B001 and the 2025 prize is a fair reason for caution, and it applies less to B048, which is not close to any recent award. On timing the clocks, I think waiting for the formal redefinition is the wrong test. The prize is for the discovery and its confirmation, which is already in hand from many laboratories, and the redefinition follows from it rather than validating it. I would welcome your view on whether the Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf credit leaves out Girvin and Huang to the point that it harms the case, because that is the fairness problem I see for B001.

responses.point: Ranks B048 first as the cleanest new-measurement-capability case, and B025 (atom interferometry) second, while noting Chu's earlier prize complicates the allocation.
responses.response: We agree on B048 and on its attribution. On B025 we also agree that it is a strong second, but I am more cautious than my ballot might suggest: the credited trio (Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich) omits Chu, whose light-pulse gravimeter and gyroscope were decisive, and the earlier laser-cooling and BEC prizes make the committee ask what is new. I therefore keep B025 as an alternative and not as a second prize part. Combining it with B048 would give five names, and I would not want to cut either list to fit three.

responses.point: Ranks the experimental Higgs discovery (B054) first as the clearest experimental discovery not yet recognised, with a three-person slate drawn from four credited names, and B048 second.
responses.response: I do not dispute the scientific weight of the Higgs discovery; it is the more consequential result for fundamental physics. My difficulty is attribution, which you yourself identify: two collaborations of thousands, four credible names and room for only three, so any selection will look arbitrary and will pass over someone with an equal claim. That does not make it unworthy, but it does mean a configuration built on B048, where the two names are not in doubt, is easier to defend. I would ask you and Ulf to say which three names you would defend if forced, since your slates differ.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; this is a judgement, not a fact I can settle.
Relative weight of Katori's 2003 proposal versus Ye's precision milestones; I rely on memory for the detailed chronology and for the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto and the Yb and Hg clock groups.
Whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (B019) or Girvin and Huang (B001) are so central that the credited sets in those candidates should be considered unfair; I cannot resolve this from my own field.
Whether a metrology achievement is read as a physics discovery by the full committee.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B048 (Katori, Ye) or B025 (Kasevich, Pritchard, Bordé). I note, for transparency, that I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and Ursula Keller (ETH) groups, but none of these is credited in any shortlisted candidate, so I do not see a need for recusal.
